program.name: Swift Agent — OSS Direction
program.description: Complete the unbuilt rungs of the adoption ladder: a hosted playground and one-click setup (scaffold CLI + managed-host deploy template), on a repaired local stack, with public-npm packaging prepared coherently but not published.

technology.playgroundHost: Fly.io or Railway (decided in WS-47) — deliberately separate from the AWS Terraform stack; must support WebSockets and pinning to exactly one instance
technology.localRegistry: Verdaccio (test-time only) for installing unpublished @swiftagent/* packages
technology.scaffoldCli: Node 22 + TypeScript, published unscoped as create-swift-agent
technology.license: Apache-2.0 (DECIDED 2026-08-19). Chosen over MIT for the explicit patent grant and patent-retaliation clause, which matter for infrastructure companies embed and deploy; it is also the norm among comparable projects. WS-44 replaces the current UNLICENSED fields and adds the repository LICENSE file.
technology.note: No changes to the runtime stack and no new runtime dependencies.

constraints.singleInstance: docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §1 and §6: connections, replay buffers, session locks, and in-flight runs are process-local; Redis pub/sub is wired but dormant; ECS is pinned to desired_count = 1. Every deployment surface this program creates must pin to exactly one instance with autoscaling disabled. Horizontal scale is Phase 2 and is out of scope.
constraints.forwardOnlyMigrations: docs/runbooks/migrations.md §1: migrations are forward-only via node packages/db/dist/migrate.js, with a drift preflight that refuses to apply on divergence. Deploy surfaces run migrate as an explicit release step; no down-migrations exist or will be added.
constraints.publishingSurfaces: Going public requires changing five agreeing surfaces together: packages/{sdk,react,shared}/package.json (publishConfig + license), a repository LICENSE file, .changeset/config.json access, docs/policies/versioning.md normative text, and scripts/verify-pack.mjs assertions.
constraints.contributionTerms: Apache-2.0 §5 licenses inbound contributions under the same outbound terms unless a contributor states otherwise, so a signed CLA is not required for the license to function. A DCO (Signed-off-by trailer, enforced in CI) is the proportionate instrument. Consequence to accept knowingly: contributors retain copyright in their contributions, so relicensing the project to different terms later would require their permission. A CLA would preserve that option at the cost of contributor friction; it is deliberately not adopted.
constraints.artifactAudience: Two distinct artifacts serve two distinct audiences: published npm packages serve the SDK consumer writing defineAgent/tool, while a published container image serves the runtime operator deploying the server. This program targets the operator, so the image is a first-class deliverable, not an optimisation. Both are release surfaces and both stay behind the same manual gate until the user audits them.
constraints.playgroundTakeaway: The playground exists to land one takeaway: "this is infrastructure, not a chat widget." It CANNOT demonstrate the product's central claim that tools run on infra the visitor controls — on a hosted demo they run on ours — so it must not imply otherwise. It proves what it can actually show, in this order: typed events you can build any UI on -> tool calls with real identity, timing, and failure semantics -> the session survives a dropped connection -> here is the code and the one command that reproduces it locally. Proving the tool boundary for real is the job of rungs 2/3 and of the proposed reverse-runner-transport program.

successCriteria.description: From a clean checkout, `docker compose up` starts Postgres, Redis, and the server; a client created against it completes a streaming turn including one tool call over WebSocket, asserted by an automated smoke check.
docker-compose.yml contains no port or PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL value that contradicts the single-listener behaviour in apps/server/src/main.ts.

@swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} declare publishConfig.registry = https://registry.npmjs.org with access: public, carry "license": "Apache-2.0" backed by a repository LICENSE file (no UNLICENSED remains), and `node scripts/verify-pack.mjs` passes with assertions updated to match.
A publish dry run succeeds for all three packages, and no workflow can upload to npm without an explicit manual trigger; demonstrated without publishing anything.
The local registry harness installs all three packages into a throwaway consumer that imports and type-checks against them, run as a repeatable command in CI.

`npx create-swift-agent <name>` (exercised against the local registry) produces a project that installs, type-checks, builds, and completes a streaming turn with a tool call, asserted end to end in CI.

The deploy template provisions the runtime with managed Postgres and Redis on the chosen host, applies forward-only migrations as an explicit release step, and passes a health check, reproducibly from the documented button or command.
The playground is reachable at a public URL and, in one session, streams tokens and surfaces at least one tool call in the event/trace panel with its start, completion, and duration.

Playground guardrails are enforced and tested: per-IP and per-session limits, a message cap, a token cap, and a global daily ceiling persisted across restarts, each producing a friendly refusal rather than an unhandled error; and the deployed instance uses a dedicated provider key carrying a provider-side budget cap, documented with its configured value.
README.md links the live playground, the deploy button, and `npx create-swift-agent`, and every ladder rung in docs/vision.md reads as built rather than planned.

No repository surface still asserts a private/restricted publishing posture: .changeset/config.json declares access: public, and docs/policies/versioning.md describes the public-npm posture accurately, including correcting its stale claim that every package is "private": true.

Every deployment surface created by this program pins to exactly one running instance with autoscaling disabled, and ships documentation citing the single-instance rationale in docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6.

A CONTRIBUTING.md and DCO file adopt the Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1 and state that contributors retain copyright; a CI check rejects a pull-request commit lacking a Signed-off-by trailer and accepts one that has it, asserted by the check actually running.

A multi-arch (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64) apps/server image builds and publishes to ghcr.io from a workflow that cannot push without an explicit manual trigger; a pulled image starts, migrates, and serves REST + WebSocket identically to a locally built one.
docker-compose.yml consumes the published image at a pinned tag rather than building the monorepo from source, and a documented override still lets contributors build locally.

The playground delivers all four demo beats, each verifiable by a visitor without reading docs: raw ChatEvent JSON is viewable beside the rendered chat; a tool call shows callId, deadline, and measured duration, and a deliberately failing tool can be triggered to show the failure path; a disconnect control drops the connection mid-stream and the session recovers; and the agent source plus the reproduce-locally command are shown on the page.

scope.summary: Makes `docker compose up` produce a genuinely working end-to-end local stack, and proves it with an automated smoke check.
includes: Repairing docker-compose.yml so published ports and PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL match the single listener on API_PORT in apps/server/src/main.ts:99
Verifying the compose-built server image starts, migrates via the existing AUTO_MIGRATE flag, and serves REST + WebSocket on one port
An automated smoke check that creates a session against the compose stack and completes one streaming turn including a tool call
Documenting the one-command local path in README.md and docs/quickstart.md
excludes: Removing or deprecating the GATEWAY_PORT env key, or changing the standalone-gateway entry point
Changing the AUTO_MIGRATE mechanism — it is real and correct (apps/server/src/config.ts:130); only ports and PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL are defective
Any change under infra/ or to the AWS deploy workflows
Changes to apps/server source beyond what a genuine, evidenced defect requires
The scaffold-generated compose file (owned by WS-46) and the managed-host deploy config (owned by WS-47)

scope.summary: Flips every repository surface from a private/restricted posture to a public Apache-2.0 project — package metadata, license, contribution terms, changesets, policy, and the pack verifier — and arms the release pipeline without firing it; no package is published.
includes: publishConfig.registry -> https://registry.npmjs.org with access: public on all three publishable packages (currently npm.pkg.github.com + restricted)
Replacing license: UNLICENSED with the decided SPDX identifier Apache-2.0 and adding the matching repository LICENSE file (none exists today)
Flipping .changeset/config.json access from restricted to public

Amending docs/policies/versioning.md §1, which normatively states packages are private and publish to a restricted registry, and which is additionally stale in claiming every package is "private": true when the three publishable packages carry no private field
Updating scripts/verify-pack.mjs, which currently asserts the GitHub Packages registry and will fail the build otherwise
Updating .github/workflows/publish-sdks.yml and publish-sdks-prerelease.yml to target npm behind an explicit manual trigger, and the CI consumer-install job that authenticates to GitHub Packages
A verified `npm publish --dry-run` for all three packages
Updating install instructions in README.md and docs/quickstart.md to state that public publishing is armed but not yet released

A CONTRIBUTING.md and a DCO file adopting the Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1, requiring a Signed-off-by trailer on every commit, with the rationale that Apache-2.0 §5 already makes contributions inbound=outbound so no CLA is required
A CI check enforcing the Signed-off-by trailer on pull-request commits, and a pull-request template prompting for it
Stating in CONTRIBUTING.md that contributors retain copyright in their contributions, so the project cannot be relicensed without their permission
excludes: Actually publishing to npm or cutting a release — explicitly deferred to a separate audit at the user's direction
Revisiting the license choice — Apache-2.0 is decided; apply it, including the NOTICE convention and the standard appendix boilerplate
Changing any package's public API surface, exports map, or build output
Reserving or configuring the npm organization account itself (a manual, human-owned step)
The local registry harness (owned by WS-45)
Adopting a CLA or any copyright-assignment agreement — deliberately rejected in favour of a DCO; do not add CLA-assistant bots or signing flows
A code of conduct, issue templates, or a docs site — still out of scope

scope.summary: Provides a local npm registry so any consumer can install @swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} as real npm dependencies before they are published.
includes: A Verdaccio-backed (or tarball-backed) local registry started and torn down by a committed script
Publishing the three packed packages into it and installing them into a throwaway consumer that imports and type-checks against them
A repeatable command wired into CI
Documentation of the harness for use by scaffold and example verification
excludes: The scaffold CLI itself and its templates (owned by WS-46) — this workstream only makes installing possible
Publishing to the real npm registry (owned by WS-44, and deferred there)
Changing packaging metadata, license fields, or the pack allowlist (owned by WS-44)
Shipping the harness as a runtime or published dependency — it is test-time only

scope.summary: Delivers `npx create-swift-agent <name>`, which scaffolds a runnable agent project — backend, frontend, and compose file — in about a minute.
includes: A new unscoped package at packages/create-swift-agent with its own build and packaging
Project templates: an SDK backend with one Zod-schema tool, a Vite/React frontend using useAgentChat, a compose file matching the WS-43 wiring, and .env.example
Interactive prompts for project name and model provider/key, with non-interactive flags for CI
An end-to-end CI test that generates a project against the WS-45 local registry, then installs, type-checks, builds, and completes a streaming turn with a tool call
Templates consuming only the public SDK surface, under the existing no-restricted-imports guard
excludes: Publishing create-swift-agent to npm (packaging is prepared; release is gated with the rest)
Deploy-target configuration for managed hosts (owned by WS-47)
The playground application (owned by WS-48) — the scaffold's template is intentionally minimal, not the demo
Repairing the root docker-compose.yml (owned by WS-43); this consumes that wiring rather than defining it
A plugin system, multiple template variants, or framework choices beyond the single canonical template

scope.summary: Lets an adopter deploy the Swift Agent runtime into their own managed-host account from a button or a single command, on exactly one pinned instance with managed Postgres and Redis attached.
includes: A documented comparison of Fly.io vs Railway against fixed criteria (managed Postgres + Redis, WebSocket support, single-instance guarantee, idle cost, template format), with the decision recorded before implementation
Host configuration (fly.toml / railway.json or equivalent) deploying the published GHCR image from WS-50 rather than building from source on the host
Pinning to exactly one running instance with autoscaling disabled, documented with the rationale from docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6
Provisioning and wiring managed Postgres and Redis, running forward-only migrations as an explicit release step per docs/runbooks/migrations.md, and passing a health check
Secret and environment documentation, including a correct public wss:// PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL
A README deploy button and a self-host guide section
A reproducible verification that a fresh deploy comes up healthy
excludes: Deploying the playground itself (owned by WS-49) — this delivers the reusable template, not the demo instance
Any change under infra/ or to the AWS dev/staging/prod Terraform stack and its workflows
Multi-instance, autoscaling, or multi-region configuration — process-local session state makes this incorrect until Phase 2
Custom domains or TLS termination beyond the host's defaults
Playground abuse controls and guest-session policy (owned by WS-49)

scope.summary: Builds the demo app around one stated takeaway — "infrastructure, not a chat widget" — delivered by four designed beats: a raw typed-event feed, a tool call with real identity and timing including its failure path, a survivable dropped connection, and the source plus the command that reproduces it locally.
includes: apps/playground/backend: an SDK agent with two to three genuinely useful tools whose calls are worth watching

BEAT 1 — typed events, not text: the event panel renders the raw ChatEvent JSON (toggleable against the prettified view) so a visitor sees message_started -> token -> tool_call_started -> tool_call_completed -> message_completed and understands they can build any UX on it

BEAT 2 — a tool call is a real round trip: surface callId, the deadline, and the measured duration; and include one tool that deliberately times out or errors, triggerable by a button, so the failure path is demonstrated rather than hidden. An infrastructure evaluator is asking "what happens when a tool hangs?" — answer it unprompted
BEAT 3 — survives a dropped connection: a disconnect control the visitor can hit mid-stream, showing the client reconnect and the session continue
BEAT 4 — the conversion beat: the ~20 lines of defineAgent/tool that produced the demo shown beside it, plus the one command that reproduces it locally

Building all four beats on the PUBLIC surface only: the vanilla createChatSession exposes onEvent() for the raw feed and disconnect() for the drop test, so compose the public client rather than extending @swiftagent/react
Guest session creation against a locally running runtime, with no signup
Consuming only the public SDK/react surface, enforced by the no-restricted-imports guard
Build, typecheck, lint, and tests green; exercised in CI like examples/quickstart
excludes: Claiming or implying that the visitor's tools run on their own infrastructure — on a hosted demo they run on ours; the copy must not overstate this, and proving it for real belongs to the proposed reverse-runner-transport program
Letting a visitor author, edit, or upload tool code — no server-side sandbox of any kind
Public deployment, the live URL, and anything requiring a hosting account (owned by WS-49)
Rate limiting, spend caps, and abuse controls (owned by WS-49) — this workstream runs locally and trusted
The deploy template itself (owned by WS-47)
New runtime, SDK, or react features. If a beat appears to need data the public surface does not expose, compose the public vanilla client or report the gap — do not add a hook or export
A marketing site, landing page, or docs site around the demo

scope.summary: Makes the playground safe to expose to the internet on the owner's model budget, deploys it publicly on a single pinned instance, and proves the live URL works.
includes: Per-IP and per-session rate limits, a per-session message cap, and a per-session token cap

A global daily spend ceiling persisted in Postgres (NOT an in-memory counter — process-local state resets on every restart per docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §1, which would silently make the ceiling per-uptime-window rather than per-day), degrading to a friendly refusal rather than an unhandled error, with tests for each limit
Short guest-session TTL and ephemeral retention configuration for the deployed instance
Deploying apps/playground to the WS-47 host target with its own database and secrets, isolated from dev/staging/prod, pinned to exactly one instance
A smoke test against the live public URL asserting a streaming turn with a visible tool call
Linking the live playground, deploy button, and scaffold command from README.md, and updating the ladder table in docs/vision.md to read as built

A dedicated model-provider API key used only by the playground, with a provider-side budget cap configured on it — the backstop that holds even if the application limiter has a bug, is bypassed, or is misconfigured; documented as a required manual setup step with the cap value
A deliberately cheap default model for the playground, chosen to minimise blast radius before any limiter fires, with the choice and its cost rationale recorded
Alerting or a documented check at a fraction of the daily ceiling, so the owner learns about unusual spend from a notification rather than from an invoice
excludes: Building the playground UI or its tools (owned by WS-48)
Authoring the deploy template (owned by WS-47) — this consumes it
Runtime-level retention modes (retention: none | metadata | full) — deliberately out of program scope; guardrails here are deployment configuration
Scaling the playground beyond one instance for load — the correct response to load is tighter caps, not more instances
Authentication, signup, or per-user accounts for the playground — it stays anonymous
Analytics, telemetry, or usage dashboards
Bring-your-own-key mode for visitors — a viable later fallback if spend proves uncomfortable, but out of scope here: the playground must stay a zero-friction 60-second demo

scope.summary: Builds and publishes the apps/server image to GHCR as the operator-facing artifact, and repoints docker-compose.yml from building the monorepo from source to pulling that image.
includes: A GitHub Actions workflow building apps/server/Dockerfile and pushing to ghcr.io, multi-arch (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64) so Apple Silicon works
A tag strategy: immutable version tags plus a moving tag, documented so operators know what they are pinning
Repointing docker-compose.yml from `build:` to `image:` at a pinned tag, with a documented compose override (or profile) so contributors can still build from source
Build provenance/attestation where the platform provides it at no extra cost
Verifying a pulled image starts, migrates, and serves REST + WebSocket exactly as the locally built one does
Operator documentation in README.md and the self-host guide: how to pull, pin, and upgrade
excludes: The first public push to GHCR — armed behind the same explicit manual trigger as npm publishing, so the user's audit covers both release surfaces; until then compose documents the build-from-source override
Publishing any image other than apps/server (no playground, scaffold, or migration images)
Changing apps/server/Dockerfile's build strategy or the --prod prune behaviour beyond what multi-arch requires
Signing infrastructure beyond what the platform offers for free (no cosign key management, no SBOM pipeline)
Repairing compose ports or PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL (owned by WS-43) — this consumes that corrected wiring
Any change under infra/ or to the ECR-based AWS deploy workflows, which continue unchanged

outOfScope: Actually publishing @swiftagent/* to public npm — deferred to a separate audit pass at the user's direction; this program arms the pipeline without firing it
Any change under infra/ (AWS Terraform stack, environments, deploy workflows)
Horizontal scaling in any form: shared session locks, shared replay buffers, cross-instance fanout, or autoscaling — Phase 2 per docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6
Runtime retention modes (retention: none | metadata | full)
Any new runtime, SDK, or react feature: no new endpoints, SDK surface, model providers, or durable execution
A hosted multi-tenant service, billing, signup, or dashboard app
Removing GATEWAY_PORT or altering the standalone-gateway entry point

A docs site, code of conduct, or issue templates — CONTRIBUTING.md and the DCO are now in scope (WS-44) because contribution terms are part of the licensing posture; the rest of the community scaffolding is not
A CLA or copyright-assignment agreement — deliberately rejected; see constraints.contributionTerms
Publishing images for anything other than apps/server, and any container signing or SBOM pipeline beyond free platform-provided provenance

An AWS Bedrock model provider — no bedrock/* provider exists in packages/models today, and adding one is explicitly not part of this program; recorded as candidate future work in docs/vision.md. The playground uses direct provider keys, which give a stronger hard spend stop than AWS Budgets do.
